We have mass spec m/z 262.09937969036, likely molecular ion [M+H]+? Usually mass spec gives m/z of molecular ion. 262.099 corresponds to formula C18H14O2 (calc mass: C18=216, H14=14.1096, O2=31.9898 total 262.0994). So formula matches.

Proton NMR: peaks: 3.83 (s, 3H) suggests methoxy group (OCH3). Then aromatic region: many protons. 7.49 (dddd, 1H), 7.66 (dddddd, 9H) seems weird 9H? maybe overlapping multiplet. 8.39 (ddddd, 1H). Total aromatic protons: 1+9+1 =11. plus 3 from OCH3 =14, matches H14.

Thus structure likely a dimethoxy biphenyl? The isomers list includes many candidates. Need to find which matches NMR pattern: a single methoxy singlet (3.83). So only one OCH3? But formula has O2, could be two O atoms: one carbonyl? But OCH3 suggests methoxy attached to aromatic, the other O maybe carbonyl (C=O) as part of ester? But then would have carbonyl carbon, maybe a methyl ester (COOCH3) would give OCH3 and carbonyl O. That would be a methyl ester. The OCH3 singlet at 3.83 typical for methyl ester. So likely a methyl ester of a polyaromatic acid.

Candidate: "COC(=O)C1=CC2C3=CC=CC=C3C1C4=CC=CC=C24" This is methyl anthracene-9-carboxylate? Actually structure: methyl anthracene-9-carboxylate (anthracene-9-carboxylate). That has one methoxy (ester) and aromatic protons. Anthracene has 14 aromatic H, but substitution reduces. Anthracene-9-carboxylate would have 10 aromatic H? Let's think: anthracene (C14H10) has 10 aromatic H. Adding CO2Me at position 9 replaces a carbon (C) with carbonyl attached, losing one H? Actually anthracene-9-carboxylic acid adds a carbonyl at central ring, replacing a hydrogen at position 9 (which originally had H). So total H becomes 9? Wait anthracene C14H10. Add CO2Me adds C2O2H3 and removes H at position 9 (since carbonyl attaches). So formula becomes C16? Let's compute: anthracene C14H10. Add CO2Me (C2H3O2) and lose H => C16H12O2? Not match. Our formula C18H14O2 suggests two extra carbons beyond anthracene (C14). So maybe a phenyl phenyl ketone? Let's examine candidates.

First candidate from isomers list: "COC1=C(C=C(C(=C1)C2=C=CC=C2)C3=C=CC=C3)OC" This is dimethoxy biphenyl? Actually has two OCH3 groups (two methoxy). That would give two singlets of 3H each, but we only see one. So not.

Second: "COC(=O)[C@]12[C@H]3[C@@H]1C4=CC=CC=C4[C@@H]3C5=CC=CC=C25" This is a chiral polycyclic ester maybe? Complex.

Third: "C=C(C1=CC=C(C=C1)C=O)C(=C)C2=CC=C(C=C2)C=O" This has aldehyde groups (C=O) not ester, would have aldehyde proton ~10 ppm, not present.

Fourth: "CC1=CC=C(C=C1)C(=O)C2=C(C=CC3=CC=CC=C32)O" This has a phenyl attached to a carbonyl and a phenol OH (O). Might have OH proton maybe broad.

Fifth: "C1=CC2=C3C(=C1)C=CC4=C(C=CC(=C43)C=C2)C(CO)O" has OH and CH2OH.

Sixth: "C1CC(=C(C2=C1C3=C(C=C2)C4=CC=CC=C4C=C3)O)O" etc.

We need a molecule with one methoxy (singlet) and aromatic protons pattern: likely a methyl ester attached to aromatic system.

Candidate: "COC(=O)C1=CC2C3=CC=CC=C3C1C4=CC=CC=C24" (the one we checked). That has one OCH3 (ester). Aromatic protons count? Anthracene core with substitution at 9 position (bridgehead). Anthracene has 14 aromatic H? Actually anthracene (C14H10) has 10 aromatic H. Wait anthracene has three fused benzene rings, formula C14H10. So 10 H. Substituting at 9 position (central carbon) replaces a hydrogen, so anthracene-9-carboxylate would have 9 aromatic H. But our NMR shows 11 aromatic H (1+9+1). That's 11 aromatic H. So maybe a phenyl phenyl system with 11 aromatic H.

Consider biphenyl with methyl ester on one phenyl: methyl 4-biphenylcarboxylate? That would have 4-phenyl-CO2Me attached to phenyl. That would have OCH3 singlet, aromatic protons: phenyl ring attached to carbonyl (para-substituted) would have 4 protons (AA'BB' pattern). The other phenyl ring unsubstituted would have 5 protons. Total 9 aromatic H. Not 11.

Maybe a naphthalene derivative with methyl ester: methyl naphthoate (methyl 1-naphthoate) would have OCH3 and naphthalene aromatic protons: naphthalene has 8 H, substitution reduces one, so 7 aromatic H. Not 11.

Our NMR shows a large multiplet of 9H at 7.66 (dddddd). That suggests overlapping of many protons, maybe two phenyl rings (5+4). Combined 9. Then additional 1H at 7.49 and 1H at 8.39 (maybe ortho to carbonyl). So total aromatic 11.

Thus maybe a phenyl phenyl ketone? But we have O2 as ester not ketone.

Could be methyl 2-phenylbenzoate? That is methyl 2-phenylbenzoate (ortho). That would have phenyl attached to benzoate ring. Aromatic protons: benzoate ring (substituted at 2 with phenyl and at 1 with CO2Me) would have 3 protons (positions 3,4,5,6? Actually ortho substitution leaves 4 protons? Let's count: benzoate ring has CO2Me at position 1, phenyl at 2, leaving positions 3,4,5,6 (4 H). Phenyl ring attached has 5 H. Total 9 aromatic H. Not 11.

Maybe methyl 4,4'-dimethyl biphenyl? No.

Let's examine other isomer candidates that have one OCH3 and aromatic protons 11.

Search list: "CC1=CC=C(C=C1)C(=O)C2=C(C=CC3=CC=CC=C32)O" has phenol OH, not OCH3.

"COC1=CC=C(C=C1)C(C#C)(C#CC2=CC=CC=C2)O" has O (hydroxy) and OCH3? Actually O attached to aromatic? Not.

"CC(=O)/C=C\\1/C(=CC2=CC=CC=C2O1)C3=CC=CC=C3" has carbonyl but not OCH3.

"COC1=CC(=C(C=C1C#C)OC)C2=CC=C(C=C2)C#C" has two OCH3.

"COC1=C(C=CC2=C1C(=CC=C2)C3=CC=CC=C3)C=O" has methoxy? Actually OCH3 attached to aromatic? "COC1=" indicates methoxy attached to aromatic, plus a carbonyl (C=O) attached to same ring (aldehyde?). That would have OCH3 and aldehyde proton ~10 ppm not present.

"COC(=O)C1=CC2C3=CC=CC=C3C1C4=CC=CC=C24" seems plausible.

Let's simulate its NMR? Could use simulate_spectra tool to compare. That would be expensive but okay maybe one call.

Let's simulate for that SMILES.
